P1.evidence: Setter named but her notes not read back — 'I know you spoke with Kyla. She kind of gave me an overview' — the same pattern as the Rafal call, which tells the prospect he was pre-qualified without showing him. Frame was two-part: 'I just want to get a good idea where you're at, you know, build out what it is that you want. And then if there's alignment, let's talk about it. If not, that's fine as well.' Agreement taken with 'All righty' / 'Yeah. Yeah.' No explicit open question was asked; the frame statement served as the invitation and the prospect launched into a three-minute self-brief, which worked but is not the scripted move.

P2.evidence: Work was covered properly and it paid off — 'I'm just thinking if there's anything else I need to go over with you, work-wise' produced the startup, the hours, the remote setup and the near-burnout admission. Weight and height were both asked directly ('How much do you weigh right now?', 'How tall are you?'); age never was. Diet asked cleanly ('What's your diet like?'). The serious failures are P2c and P2d: no health condition question and no injury or movement-limitation question at any point in a 37-minute call that ended with a recommendation to start loaded ballistic training. Sleep and energy were also never asked, which is the costly one here — the prospect volunteered 'I'm sort of almost at that burnout stage... on the weekends, I'll just spend time just sleeping because I'm just extremely exhausted', and the rep responded with 'You've got to find a bit of balance in those moments' and moved on.

P3.evidence: Much the strongest phase in the batch. The trigger-point question ran properly — 'what was the trigger point for you to say I'm actually going to do something about it and take it more seriously?' — and produced the real driver: turning 40 and a first child. He then asked directly about the family timeline ('are you trying for a baby at the moment with your partner?') and followed with the best single question anywhere in this batch: 'If you had a five-year-old son right now... what example do you feel like you'd be setting for him?' That drove straight through to legacy and identity and got a genuinely reflective answer. Good clarifying reflect-back on the goal itself — 'Is it more about the weight or more about the composition?' — which correctly reframed the goal from weight to strength, and 'Basketball is kind of like your reference point for healthy.'

P4.evidence: Not run. 'I've never had a trainer before' and 'Last year was like zero gym for me' both came out of the prospect's opening monologue, unprompted, and were never opened up — no 'what happened with that', no 'why do you feel it didn't stick', no 'the information isn't the problem'. The structural gap was named by the prospect himself ('I always put off just fitness in general', 'I just want to build the habits again and hopefully stay with it') rather than surfaced by the rep. Given that the prospect already owns kettlebells sitting unused in the room behind him, the single most available root-cause question in the call — why haven't you used them — was never asked.

P5.evidence: Partial credit for the hypothetical-son question, which functions as a cost-of-inaction frame and did land: the prospect answered with his own two-year picture — 'if I don't get those habits, whilst I'm sitting in my 30s, like, my [40s] are gonna be extremely difficult.' But the rep never converted it. He responded 'Well, the good news is you have the power to change it, brother' and moved on. No 'is that something you're willing to settle for', no 'why not', no line in the sand. The prospect had handed over a hard deadline — a child arriving next year — and it was never used as leverage on the decision.

P6.evidence: Only weak tie-downs ran. 'Are you willing to set aside four hours a week?' got a qualified yes, and 'Does it align?' got 'Yeah, I'll say to a great extent it does. Of course, I need to do some thinking on that.' The belief question in its scripted form was never asked — the rep asserted it instead ('I know we can get you where you want to go'). P6b was never asked at all, so nothing was isolated. P6c is a clear fail: 'I need to do some thinking on that' is hesitation and the script says return to Phase 5; the rep went to the guarantee and the price.

P11.evidence: Unreachable. The price was given in response to the prospect's own question and the rep never asked for the business, so no payment, onboarding booking, agreement or welcome-email step was in play. Unlike the other two sales calls in this batch, the Trevor onboarding sequence was not even pre-framed.

objection_plays.detail: 'Obviously, I have a lot to think about on this' and 'I'll say about a week' is the trigger, and not one of the seven scripted moves ran. No 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to your goal', no 'what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no decision-pattern challenge. Worse than absent — the rep actively reinforced the deferral: 'I'm not going to tell you not to do it', 'the most important thing is just committing to something', 'if you want to do it you can reach back out to me.'

Value against a cheaper functioning alternative — an in-person personal trainer at a gym sixteen minutes' walk away. This is the second known gap already recorded in the playbook from the Badrane Hriouch call, recurring with a prospect who had no affordability objection at all. The rep engaged substantively and honestly: a structured pros-and-cons of in-person versus online, the async-video rationale for why coaching calls were dropped, and the Steph Curry versus LeBron James's son analogy for coach quality. But with no scripted path he defaulted to neutrality and conceded ground he did not have to concede, volunteering that the trainer would be cheaper and supplying a price for it ('probably 50 quid for a session'). A script asset is needed here: the head-to-head is winnable on schedule fit, at-home training and the exit-by-design model, all three of which the prospect himself named as what stood out.

No money objection arose at any point. The prospect asked the fee structure as a neutral question ('What's the fee structure for the program?') and did not react to £4,500 beyond 'Oh. That makes sense.' Recorded explicitly because the absence matters: the one call in this batch with no affordability barrier is also the one where the rep did not ask for the sale.

notes: P3 was excellent and everything downstream of it was given away. The rep surfaced a first child, a fortieth birthday and a near-burnout admission — three separate levers — then used none of them, skipped P4 entirely, left P5 half-run, took hesitation as an answer at P6 and never asked for the business. On the cheaper-alternative objection he was scrupulously fair to the point of selling against himself, quoting the competitor's price unprompted. The concrete coaching points: ask health and injury questions on every call without exception, convert the consequence frame into a commitment rather than a compliment ('you have the power to change it'), and stop conceding the comparison when the prospect has already told you which three things make you the better fit.
